leads.candidate: The 1835 Ginkgo near the Joy Street steps, Boston Common
leads.why_a_lead: Per Friends of the Public Garden, the first ginkgo in Boston's parks was transplanted to the Common near the Joy Street steps in 1835, already 40 feet tall at the time, moved from the estate of Mrs. Gardiner Greene (daughter of John Singleton Copley). That would make it a genuinely remarkable, historically documented tree, with a real minimum age (already 40ft when moved in 1835 implies decades of growth before that, likely pushing true age past 200 years). Re-checked this pass: still could not confirm this specific 1835 individual is still standing, which of the Common's 13 ginkgos it is, or a mappable location beyond 'near the Joy Street steps'; general web search turns up nothing more specific than the same FoPG article. Needs a dedicated look (Friends of the Public Garden tree inventory/map, an arborist record, or an in-person/photo check against the Joy Street steps) to confirm it survives and pin it.

leads.candidate: The last true American Elm on the Common, Railroad Mall
leads.why_a_lead: Friends of the Public Garden identifies this as 'the last true, non-hybridized, American Elm on the Common', located on Railroad Mall just west of the Visitor Information Center. Historically significant (Massachusetts state tree, once-common species nearly wiped out by Dutch Elm Disease, which reached New England in the 1930s-40s, so a genuine survivor is at minimum mature by then). Read the full FoPG 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' article this pass: it is a general educational piece about the elm collection across all three parks, not an individual specimen profile, and gives no planting date or age for this tree specifically, only its location and rarity. Targeted web search for a second source (news coverage, Boston Parks Dept, a specific age) found nothing beyond the same FoPG page. Still single-sourced on age; stays a lead rather than shipping with a guessed age.

leads.candidate: American Elm pair, Public Garden, east of the Marvin Goody Flagpole along Charles St.
leads.why_a_lead: Described by Friends of the Public Garden as large specimens, in the same general 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' article as the Railroad Mall elm above. Same problem: no age given anywhere in the source, and being a pair raises the collectible-point question (would need one obvious place to stand, which a flagpole-adjacent pair plausibly offers, but unverified). No second source found this pass.

leads.candidate: Second Dawn Redwood, Public Garden, Boylston Street end of the Lagoon
leads.why_a_lead: Friends of the Public Garden's dawn redwood article mentions a second, older specimen: re-read closely this pass, the text is genuinely ambiguous about which of the two Public Garden redwoods was planted in 1963. It describes the Charles/Beacon specimen (the article's main subject) as standing 'near an older sibling across the path... planted in 1963', which could mean either that the sibling (not the Charles/Beacon tree) is the 1963 one, or that both are being described together. bos_004, already published, states flatly that IT (at Charles/Beacon) was planted 1963. This is worth a second look by whoever next touches bos_004 or this lead: if the 1963 date actually belongs to the 'older sibling' tree elsewhere near the Lagoon (the text separately places a Boylston St end redwood near a bald cypress across the path from it), bos_004's location or the second redwood's identity may need correcting. Not resolved or acted on this pass since it touches an already-published tree, outside a verify pass's remit to edit; flagging for a city-file review instead.

leads.candidate: Rock Elm near the Tool Shed, Public Garden
leads.why_a_lead: Called out by Friends of the Public Garden as 'the lone specimen in the three parks' (Common, Public Garden, Commonwealth Ave Mall), which makes it a genuinely singular, collectible point in principle, and the species itself is notably long-lived (up to ~300 years per general references). Same FoPG 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' source as above, still no age given for this individual. Checked the Arnold Arboretum's own Arnoldia piece on the species ('Ulmus thomasii: The Hard Elm That's Hard to Find', 2016) as a possible second source; it discusses the species generally and the Arboretum's own specimens, not the Public Garden tree, so it doesn't corroborate this individual. Stays a lead.

leads.candidate: Mount Auburn Cemetery champion trees (28 state champions, 11 New England champions)
leads.why_a_lead: Mount Auburn (Cambridge/Watertown line) is an accredited Level III Arboretum with over 5,300 trees inventoried (1997) including 28 Massachusetts state champions and 11 New England champions, per the cemetery's own 'Champion Trees of Mount Auburn' program. Transit checked this pass: subway plus the 71 bus from downtown Boston runs about 29 minutes per Rome2rio, or Red Line to Harvard Square (Boston Common to Harvard is itself a good chunk of that) then the 71/73 bus roughly 16 minutes, or a 15-20 minute walk from Harvard Square along Brattle St into Mount Auburn St. So it sits right on the ~30 minute day-trip boundary in the optimistic case and over it once real transfer waits are counted; label honestly as 'about 30-40 minutes from downtown Boston via Harvard Square' rather than claiming it clears the bar cleanly. Still could not identify a single named, individually pinnable champion tree with species and age in this pass: the cemetery's own tree-map/flyer (mountauburn.pastperfectonline.com, keyword 'Tree Map') needs a dedicated fetch, and the 'Champion Trees of Mount Auburn' guided-walk materials were not reachable as plain text in the time available. Checked one specific named tree, the Prince of Wales Beech (see below): historically the most famous individual specimen here, but it is a 2008-planted graft, not the 1860 original, so it fails 'genuinely old' outright even though it would pass 'historically significant'. Per the brief: never pin 'the cemetery' as a tree; this stays a lead until a specific living, aged, individually locatable specimen turns up.

leads.candidate: The Prince of Wales Beech, Mount Auburn Cemetery
leads.why_a_lead: Genuinely remarkable story: planted by the 19-year-old Prince of Wales (future Edward VII) in person on 19 October 1860, a well-documented royal-visit tree with contemporary newspaper coverage. But the original tree developed Beech Tree Decline, was sonically imaged in 2007 (over 50% of trunk wood unsound) and was removed in March 2008 at more than 150 years old. What stands today, planted in a ceremony on 3 May 2008, is a single surviving scion grafted from 1993 cuttings of the original, roughly 18 years old now, genetically identical but not the tree the Prince touched. Under the project's living-succession rule this could ship as an entry describing the living graft honestly (comparable to the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent), but a barely-18-year-old sapling is a stretch for 'ancient trees' and reads better as a story footnote than a collectible point; leaving it as a lead rather than forcing it in. Also unresolved: Mount Auburn's day-trip transit status (see the champion-trees entry above).

leads.candidate: Tree Boston 'Big Old Trees Program' entries (Roxbury Willow at Fort Hill, Dorchester Ginkgo at 31 Tonawanda St, Mattapan Swamp White Oak, East Boston Willow, Hyde Park Pin Oak at Fairview Cemetery)
leads.species: various (Salix alba, Ginkgo biloba, Quercus bicolor, Quercus palustris)
leads.why_a_lead: treeboston.org runs a crowd-nominated 'Big Old Trees' registry with addresses and trunk diameter (DBH) for each: Roxbury Willow (20 Fort Ave, DBH 52in, height 42ft), Dorchester Ginkgo (31 Tonawanda St, DBH 41.5in, height 93.7ft), Mattapan Swamp White Oak (201-211 River St, DBH 42in), East Boston Willow (East Boston Memorial Ballpark, DBH 46in), Hyde Park Pin Oak (45 Fairview Ave, Fairview Cemetery, DBH 44in). Re-fetched in full this pass (treeboston.org loads fine with a browser user agent, unlike universalhub.com below): confirmed none carry an age estimate anywhere on the page, only DBH/height, and the registry is explicitly self-reported/nomination-based rather than professionally dated. Estimating age from DBH alone without a species-specific growth-rate source would be a guess dressed as a fact, so still not verifiable on age. They are also scattered across outer Boston neighbourhoods rather than forming a walkable cluster. Each would need an actual age source (arborist record, core sample, planting record) and a second confirming source before it could verify.

leads.candidate: Wilson's Japanese Black Pines, Peters Hill Road, Arnold Arboretum (accessions 11371*J, 11371*M, 11371*O)
leads.why_a_lead: Three sibling trees grown from seed E.H. Wilson acquired from the Yokohama Nursery Company at the very end of his 1917-1919 expedition, planted along Peters Hill Road curling uphill from the Peters Hill Gate; 11371*J turned 100 in 2019 (Arnoldia 'New Year's Elders'), 11371*O is described on the Arboretum's own plant-bio page as smaller and more contorted, a sibling of the same seed lot. Confirmed alive and on display, well documented, distinctive picturesque wind-bent form. Not delivered this pass because both sources trace to the Arboretum itself (Arnoldia story plus plant-bios page) with no independent confirmation found (a Harvard Art Museums piece on a Jakuchu painting references 'the arboretum's rich history and the live specimen' but does not name which tree or give any identifying details), and because two other Arboretum trees (bos_007 bonsai, bos_008 katsura) were already delivered this pass; adding a third would tip the city further toward being an Arboretum showcase. A strong candidate for a later pass, ideally paired with an independent source search (local news, a garden-tour writeup) rather than more Arboretum-authored pages.

leads.candidate: Mount Auburn Cemetery and Forest Hills Cemetery, specific named champion/specimen trees
leads.why_a_lead: Checked again this pass with fresh searches for a single named, individually locatable specimen at either cemetery. Mount Auburn: the 'Champion Trees of Mount Auburn' event page still names no individual tree, species or location, only that 'some of the Massachusetts Champions' are on the grounds; the cemetery's own tree-map database (mountauburn.pastperfectonline.com) was not reachable as a searchable list in the time available. Forest Hills Cemetery (in Jamaica Plain, actually within Boston city limits, so it would clear the day-trip question that Mount Auburn does not): general sources describe 'an unusual collection of large specimen trees, some introduced by the Arnold Arboretum' including cherry, sugar and Japanese maple, umbrella pine and weeping hemlock, but nothing names a single tree with location or age. Both stay leads until a dedicated fetch of the actual tree-map/inventory tools turns up one specific, pinnable specimen.

leads.candidate: The Washington Elm successor sapling, Cambridge Common
leads.why_a_lead: The original Washington Elm (Garden St / Mason St junction, where Washington supposedly took command of the Continental Army in 1775) died and was removed in 1923; a bronze marker set flush in the pavement is all that is confirmed to remain there (per History Cambridge's dedicated 'Washington Elm Debate Rages On' article, fetched in full this pass). A general web search snippet separately claimed 'a sapling of the iconic elm was planted in the Common by Vice President Charles Dawes on April 19, 1925, and that tree is the one that stands in Cambridge Common today', but the History Cambridge article itself, which covers the same 1925 sesquicentennial commemoration in detail, describes only a parade and the bronze plaque, concluding 'now nothing remains'. Genuinely contradictory between a search-engine summary and the dedicated primary source; not resolved this pass. If a Dawes sapling was in fact planted in 1925 and survives, it would be a ~101-year-old tree and a strong day-trip-boundary-clearing (Cambridge Common is central, no transit issue) candidate under the living-succession precedent. Needs a dedicated look at Cambridge Common's own tree inventory or the Cambridge Historical Commission before shipping either way.

Logged as a fresh clue for whoever next works this lead rather than acted on; not enough to pin or verify this pass.
